```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

rm(list = ls())
if (rstudioapi::isAvailable()) {
  setwd(dirname(rstudioapi::getActiveDocumentContext()$path))
}

out_dir <- "../../output/5_inference_final"
topic_path <- "../../input/topics/topic_labels.csv"

fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")

# Dataset size, from the per-(thread, model, method) cell table written by
# 3e_filter_and_balance.py: synthetic comments per cell and the thread's real
# comment count.
cells <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "qc_filter_and_balance.csv"))
n_threads <- n_distinct(cells$post_id)
n_synth <- sum(cells$original_n)
n_real <- sum(distinct(cells, post_id, real_count)$real_count)
n_synth_weight <- sum(pmin(cells$original_n, cells$real_count))
n_models <- n_distinct(cells$model)
n_methods <- n_distinct(cells$method)

# Topic labels (collaborator's pipeline), one row per thread.
topics <- read.csv(topic_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
RESIDUAL <- c("Nonmedical", "Medical; other")
EXPLORATORY_BELOW <- 0.05
topic_tbl <- topics %>%
  count(discipline, name = "threads") %>%
  mutate(share = threads / sum(threads),
         role = case_when(discipline %in% RESIDUAL ~ "Left out (residual category)",
                          share < EXPLORATORY_BELOW ~ "Included, exploratory (< 5% of threads)",
                          TRUE ~ "Included")) %>%
  arrange(desc(threads))
n_topics_in <- sum(!topic_tbl$discipline %in% RESIDUAL)
n_expl <- sum(topic_tbl$role == "Included, exploratory (< 5% of threads)")
n_threads_in <- sum(topic_tbl$threads[!topic_tbl$discipline %in% RESIDUAL])
n_cancer <- sum(tolower(topics$cancer_relevant) == "true", na.rm = TRUE)
n_cancer_na <- sum(!tolower(topics$cancer_relevant) %in% c("true", "false"))
topic_md5 <- unname(tools::md5sum(topic_path))
```

# In short

Earlier analyses showed that comments written by AI models generally show
less empathy than the real clinician comments they imitate, with some
exceptions. This report asks a follow-up question: **is that gap the same for every kind of medical
question, or is it bigger for some topics (say, mental health) than for
others (say, skin conditions)?**

To find out, every one of the `r fmt(n_threads)` Reddit r/AskDocs threads in
the study was assigned a medical topic based on the original post, and we
then estimated how the real-vs-AI empathy gap changes from topic to topic.
We did this with a statistical model that is deliberately cautious about
small topics: it estimates each topic's gap, but pulls estimates for topics
with little data toward the overall average rather than letting a handful of
threads produce a dramatic-looking result.

We also asked a second, simpler question: **do threads where cancer is
involved look different from the rest?**

Results will be added below once the models have finished running.

# What we did, in plain terms

## The comparison

Each thread is a patient's question posted on r/AskDocs. For each thread we
have the comments that real, verified clinicians wrote, and comments that
`r n_models` AI models wrote in response to the same post, using
`r n_methods` different prompting strategies. In total that is
`r fmt(n_real)` real comments and `r fmt(n_synth)` AI-written ones.

Each comment was rated by three trained classifiers for three kinds of
empathy: **emotional reactions** (acknowledging how the patient feels),
**interpretations** (showing the patient's situation was understood), and
**explorations** (asking about or probing the patient's experience). Each
rating is "none", "weak", or "strong". Comments with some empathy are fairly
rare, so the models below ask a simple yes/no question: *does this comment
show this kind of empathy?*

## Assigning a topic to every thread

A language model read the title and text of each opening post and chose one of
17 medical disciplines (for example Dermatology, Cardiovascular, Psychiatry
and mental health). The label belongs to the **thread**, so every comment
under a post, real or AI-written, carries that post's topic.

Two of the 17 labels are catch-alls, "Medical; other" and "Nonmedical". They
describe what a post is *not* rather than what it is, so we left them out of
the topic analysis. Table \@ref(tab:topics) shows how many threads fall in
each topic. `r n_expl` topics are small (under 5% of threads); they stay in
the analysis, but are flagged as exploratory.

```{r topics}
topic_tbl %>%
  mutate(share = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * share), threads = fmt(threads)) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Topic", "Threads", "Share of threads", "Role in the topic analysis"),
        align = c("l", "r", "r", "l"),
        caption = "Threads per topic and how each topic is used.")
```

## Making a fair comparison

Two features of the data would distort a naive comparison.

- **Comments from the same thread are not independent.** A thread about a
  frightening symptom might draw more empathetic replies of both kinds. The
  model accounts for this by giving every thread its own baseline.
- **There are more AI comments than real ones in a thread.** The AI models
  wrote one reply for every comment on a thread, but only some of those
  comments came from verified clinicians. Without correction, threads with
  many comments would count for more on the AI side than on the real side. We
  fixed this by *weighting* rather than discarding data: a real comment counts
  as 1, and when a model wrote more comments for a thread than there are real
  ones, each of its comments counts for a fraction, so that for every thread
  both sides carry the same total weight. For example, if a thread has 2
  real comments and one model wrote 8, each of those 8 counts for 0.25.

We looked at two other options before choosing this. Dropping AI comments
that were unusually long or short removed comments that showed empathy
unevenly across the models, and left some threads without enough AI comments
to match the real ones. Randomly keeping only as many AI comments as real
ones made the results depend noticeably on which comments happened to be
kept. Weighting avoids both problems.

## Letting the gap differ by topic

For each type of empathy, the model estimates:

1. how much less likely an AI comment is to show empathy than a real one, on
   average (the **gap**), and
2. how much each topic moves that gap up or down (the topic's **shift**).

The topic shifts are *partially pooled*: a topic with many threads gets an
estimate that is mostly its own, while a topic with few threads is pulled
toward the average. This is the main protection against over-reading small
topics, and it means we do not need a separate cut-off or a correction for
looking at many topics.

The question about cancer is handled by a separate, simpler model that
compares the gap in the `r fmt(n_cancer)` cancer-related threads with the
gap in all other threads.

## How to read the numbers

Everything is reported as an **odds ratio** with a 95% credible interval.

- A *gap* below 1 means AI comments have lower odds of showing empathy than
  real ones. A gap of 0.5 means the odds are halved.
- A *shift* is relative to the average topic. Below 1 means the gap is
  *larger* than average in that topic; above 1 means *smaller*.
- `pd` is the probability, given the data and model, that the effect points
  the way we report it. It is not a p-value. We call a result **credible**
  only when `pd` is above 0.975 *and* the interval excludes 1.

# What to keep in mind

- **The topic labels are imperfect.** The labelling model agrees with a
  reference set of 200 posts about 77% of the time, and the reference set was
  itself mostly produced by language models. Roughly one label in four may be
  off. Errors in a grouping variable like this blur real differences, so a
  finding of "no topic differences" is weaker evidence than it sounds.
- **Topic comes from the post, not the comment.** A reply that wanders to a
  different subject still carries the original post's topic.
- **The gap is an average over the AI models and strategies.** These differ
  a lot from one another, and for some empathy types they do not even point
  the same way (for Interpretations, Grok's comments score above the real
  ones while Gemini's and OpenAI's score below), so the average can look
  small where individual models differ strongly. The topic shift is assumed
  to be the same for all of them; we have not tested whether topics affect
  some models more than others.
- **Empathy ratings come from classifiers, not people.** All comparisons are
  about what the classifiers detect.
- **Weighting is an approximation.** It targets the same quantity as
  repeated random sampling would, but the reported uncertainty is only
  approximate.
- **Small topics are exploratory.** Even with pooling, topics with few
  threads give wide intervals.

# Methods {#methods}

## Data

The analysis uses all `r fmt(n_real + n_synth)` rated comments from
`r fmt(n_threads)` threads (`r fmt(n_real)` real, `r fmt(n_synth)` synthetic),
with no outlier exclusion and no subsampling. Synthetic comments come from
Gemini, OpenAI and Grok, each under three prompting strategies: DG
(discourse generation), SAG (single advice generation) and SAGII (SAG with
incremental information). That gives nine synthetic groups plus the real
group.

Empathy labels (0 = none, 1 = weak, 2 = strong) for emotional reactions
(ER), interpretations (IP) and explorations (EX) come from three fine-tuned
RoBERTa bi-encoder classifiers following the EPITOME framework. The binary
outcome is `label >= 1` for ER. For IP and EX the classifiers never output
label 1 in this data, so `label >= 1` and `label == 2` coincide. The
three-level ER outcome used in the main Bayesian models is not used here: split by topic its
strong-empathy cell is nearly empty for some models (for Grok, a handful of
comments out of about 14,000), so the binary collapse is used instead.

## Topic labels

Labels were produced by the collaborators' pipeline (`classify_topics.py`):
an LLM (gemini-2.5-pro, temperature 0) assigns each opening post to one of 17
disciplines from the taxonomy in Chan et al. (JMIR Formative Research 2025;
9:e55309). There is one label per thread, joined on `submission_id`; all
`r fmt(n_threads)` threads are labelled. The `discipline` column is used
for every thread (not the reference-sample labels), so that measurement is
uniform across the corpus. The file used has md5
`r topic_md5` (`input/topics/SOURCE.txt` records its origin).

Validation against a 200-post reference sample: production-model agreement
0.770; agreement between the two LLM annotators who built the reference
0.795 (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.779), with a human adjudicating their
disagreements. The reference is therefore mainly inter-model consensus.

The topic models use the `r n_topics_in` substantive disciplines
(`r fmt(n_threads_in)` threads). "Medical; other" and "Nonmedical" are
excluded from them but kept in the other analyses. Topics with under
`r 100 * EXPLORATORY_BELOW`% of threads (`r n_expl` of the `r n_topics_in`) are
flagged exploratory in the outputs but remain in the model, where partial
pooling governs their estimates.

## Response weights

Let $n_c$ be the number of synthetic comments in a (thread, model, method)
cell and $r$ the thread's number of real comments. A real comment has weight
1 and a synthetic comment has weight $w = \min(1, r / n_c)$. The synthetic
weights sum to `r fmt(n_synth_weight)`, which is exactly what random
per-thread subsampling to $\min(n_c, r)$ would retain, and the expected
subsampled log-likelihood equals the weighted one. Weights are computed
on all threads before any topic filtering, so excluding threads does not
change the weights of the rest. In `brms` the weights multiply each
observation's log-likelihood, giving a pseudo-likelihood: point estimates
target the subsampling average, but posterior widths are approximate.

## Models

Fitted separately for ER, IP and EX with a Bernoulli likelihood and logit
link, $y_i$ the binary outcome, $s_i$ an indicator for a synthetic comment,
$g(i)$ the comment's group (real or one of nine model-by-method cells),
$t(i)$ its thread's topic and $p(i)$ its thread:

**Model C (topic moderation).**
$$\operatorname{logit} P(y_i = 1) = \alpha + \beta_{g(i)} + \gamma\,\log(\text{length}_i) + u_{t(i)} + v_{t(i)}\,s_i + a_{p(i)}$$
with $(u_t, v_t) \sim \mathcal N(0, \Sigma)$ over topics and
$a_p \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma_p^2)$ over threads. The $\beta_g$ are the group
coefficients as in the main analysis. A topic's gap on the log-odds scale is
the mean of the nine synthetic $\beta_g$ plus $v_t$; its *shift* is $v_t$;
both are exponentiated to odds ratios. The posterior of the SD of $v_t$ is
the direct measure of how much the gap varies by topic. A random slope on the
single indicator $s$ (rather than on the nine groups) keeps the covariance
structure small enough to estimate from 15 topics.

**Model D (cancer relevance).**
$$\operatorname{logit} P(y_i = 1) = \alpha + \beta_{g(i)} + \delta\,c_{p(i)} + \theta\,s_i c_{p(i)} + \gamma\,\log(\text{length}_i) + a_{p(i)}$$
where $c$ indicates a cancer-relevant thread. The gap is the mean of the
synthetic $\beta_g$ for non-cancer threads and that plus $\theta$ for cancer
threads; $\theta$ is the moderation. The `r n_cancer_na` threads with no cancer
flag are dropped from this model only.

## Priors and sampling

Fixed effects: Normal(0, 2.5), the standard weakly-informative default for
logistic models (Gelman et al., 2008); this also keeps estimates finite in
sparse cells. Intercept and the thread SD: Student-$t$(3, 0, 2.5). Topic SDs
(intercept and slope): Normal(0, 1) truncated at zero, tighter because 15
topics carry little information about a variance. The topic correlation uses
`brms`' default LKJ(1) prior.

Models are fitted with `brms` (Stan via `cmdstanr`): 4 chains of 2,000
iterations (1,000 warmup), 4 threads per chain, `adapt_delta` = 0.95, seed
20260101. A fit is accepted as converged when max $\hat R < 1.01$, the
minimum effective-sample-size ratio exceeds 0.1, and there are no divergent
transitions; this is reported per fit. The Interpretations topic model
(Model C) was rerun with 4,000 iterations because its max $\hat R$ was
1.0106 at 2,000; this brought it to 1.003 but left one divergent transition
in 8,000 draws, and its estimates and the set of credible topics were
unchanged. Multithreaded summation makes draws
non-reproducible from the seed alone, so the fitted models are saved to disk
(`models_bayesian/`) together with software versions
(`run_metadata_topic.txt`) and reproducibility rests on those.

## Reporting

For each quantity: posterior median odds ratio, 95% highest-density interval,
and $pd = \max\{P(\theta > 0), P(\theta < 0)\}$ on the log-odds scale.
"Credible" requires $pd > 0.975$ and an interval excluding 1. No frequentist
multiplicity correction is applied; topic-level estimates are partially
pooled instead. Topics under 5% of threads are labelled exploratory. Code:
`3h_topic_moderation_models.R`.

## Known limitations of the design

- Misclassification of the topic moderator attenuates moderation estimates
  toward zero; no correction for it is applied.
- The topic shift is common to all nine synthetic groups. Whether it differs
  across models or methods is a separate model, not fitted here.
- The cancer flag is a separate construct from the "Neoplasms" topic (which
  also covers benign neoplasms and requires a clinician or test to have
  raised the concern).
- Weighted posterior intervals are approximate; a subsampling sensitivity
  check is planned separately.

# Results {#results}

```{r results-setup}
mech_names <- c(ER = "Emotional Reactions", IP = "Interpretations", EX = "Explorations")
CREDIBLE_PD <- 0.975
conv <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "topic_convergence.csv"))
sdt <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "topic_sd_summary.csv"))
canc <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "topic_cancer_moderation.csv"))
all_topic <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "topic_gap_by_topic.csv"))
avg <- all_topic %>% filter(topic == "(average over topics)")
bt <- all_topic %>% filter(topic != "(average over topics)") %>%
  mutate(credible = shift_pd > CREDIBLE_PD & (shift_lcl > 1 | shift_ucl < 1))

f1 <- function(x) ifelse(x < 0.1, sprintf("%.3f", x), sprintf("%.2f", x))
or3 <- function(m, l, u) sprintf("%s (%s-%s)", f1(m), f1(l), f1(u))
n_est <- nrow(bt)
n_cred <- sum(bt$credible)
conv_ok <- all(conv$converged)
```

## Model checks

`r if (conv_ok) sprintf("All %d fits met the convergence criteria (largest max Rhat %.4f, smallest effective-sample-size ratio %.3f, no divergent transitions).", nrow(conv), max(conv$max_rhat), min(conv$min_neff_ratio)) else sprintf("%d of %d fits met every convergence criterion; the exception is: %s.", sum(conv$converged), nrow(conv), toString(vapply(which(!conv$converged), function(k) { r <- conv[k, ]; sprintf("%s %s (%s)", mech_names[r$mechanism], c(C_topic_gap = "topic model", D_cancer = "cancer model")[r$model], toString(c(if (r$max_rhat >= 1.01) sprintf("max Rhat %.4f", r$max_rhat), if (r$min_neff_ratio <= 0.1) sprintf("ESS ratio %.3f", r$min_neff_ratio), if (isTRUE(r$divergent_transitions > 0)) sprintf("%d divergent transition%s", r$divergent_transitions, ifelse(r$divergent_transitions > 1, "s", ""))))) }, character(1))))`

## Does the gap vary by topic?

Table \@ref(tab:sd) gives the average gap for each empathy type and how much
it moves from topic to topic. The spread is the
standard deviation of the topic shifts on the log-odds scale; a spread of
$s$ means a typical topic's gap is a factor of $e^{s}$ above or below the
average.

```{r sd}
sd_slope <- sdt %>% filter(parameter == "topic_slope_sd")
tab <- avg %>%
  transmute(mechanism, avg_gap = or3(gap_or, gap_lcl, gap_ucl)) %>%
  left_join(sd_slope %>% transmute(mechanism, spread = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f-%.2f)", median, lcl, ucl),
                                   factor = sprintf("x%.2f", exp(median))), by = "mechanism") %>%
  mutate(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism])
kable(tab, col.names = c("Empathy type", "Average gap, odds ratio (95% CrI)",
                         "Spread across topics, SD (95% CrI)", "Typical factor"),
      align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Average real-vs-AI gap and how much it varies across topics.")
```

`r sprintf("The interval for the spread lies clearly above zero (lower end above 0.05) for %d of %d empathy types, so the gap does differ across topics, by an amount that depends on the empathy type. ", sum(sd_slope$lcl > 0.05), nrow(sd_slope))`Gaps below 1
mean AI comments have lower odds of showing empathy than real ones.
`r near1 <- avg %>% filter(gap_lcl < 1, gap_ucl > 1); if (nrow(near1) > 0) sprintf("For %s the average gap's interval includes 1: on average AI comments are roughly on par with real ones there, and individual topics fall on either side.", toString(mech_names[near1$mechanism])) else ""`

## Which topics differ?

Figure \@ref(fig:forest) shows every topic's gap; filled points are topics
whose shift from the average is credible.

```{r forest, fig.width=9, fig.height=6.5, fig.cap="Real-vs-AI gap by topic (odds ratio, log scale; below 1 = AI comments less likely to show empathy). Filled points: credible shift from the average. Starred topics have under 5% of threads (exploratory). Dashed line: no gap; dotted line: average over topics."}
plot_df <- bt %>%
  mutate(mechanism = factor(mech_names[mechanism], levels = unname(mech_names)),
         label = paste0(discipline, ifelse(exploratory, " *", "")),
         label = factor(label, levels = unique(label[order(n_threads)])))
avg_df <- avg %>% mutate(mechanism = factor(mech_names[mechanism], levels = unname(mech_names)))
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = gap_or, y = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(data = avg_df, aes(xintercept = gap_or), linetype = "dotted", colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = gap_lcl, xmax = gap_ucl), height = 0, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = credible, fill = credible), size = 2.6, colour = "black") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 21, `FALSE` = 21), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "black", `FALSE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~mechanism, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Gap: odds ratio, AI vs. real (95% credible interval)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

`r n_cred` of the `r n_est` topic-level shifts are credible
(Table \@ref(tab:credible)). Shifts above 1 mean the gap is smaller than
average in that topic; below 1, larger.

```{r credible}
cr <- bt %>% filter(credible) %>%
  arrange(match(mechanism, names(mech_names)), desc(n_threads)) %>%
  transmute(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism],
            topic = paste0(discipline, ifelse(exploratory, " *", "")),
            threads = n_threads,
            gap = or3(gap_or, gap_lcl, gap_ucl),
            shift = or3(shift_or, shift_lcl, shift_ucl),
            pd = sprintf("%.3f", shift_pd))
if (nrow(cr) > 0) {
  kable(cr, col.names = c("Empathy type", "Topic", "Threads", "Gap, OR (95% CrI)", "Shift, OR (95% CrI)", "pd"),
        align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
        caption = "Topics whose gap credibly differs from the average (starred topics are exploratory).")
} else {
  cat("No topic-level shift is credible.")
}
```

These should be read as leads rather than conclusions. With `r n_est`
shifts examined, around `r sprintf("%.0f", 0.05 * n_est)` would clear a
threshold like this by chance alone even if topic made no difference
(partial pooling reduces this, but does not remove it). The topic labels are
also noisy, which blurs real differences. Topics under 5% of threads give
wide intervals and are the least trustworthy.

## Cancer-related threads

```{r cancer, results='asis'}
for (i in seq_len(nrow(canc))) {
  r <- canc[i, ]
  cred <- r$shift_pd > CREDIBLE_PD & (r$shift_lcl > 1 | r$shift_ucl < 1)
  dir <- ifelse(r$shift_or > 1, "smaller", "larger")
  cat(sprintf("- **%s:** gap %s in other threads and %s in cancer-related threads. %s\n",
              mech_names[r$mechanism],
              f1(r$gap_not_cancer_or),
              or3(r$gap_cancer_or, r$gap_cancer_lcl, r$gap_cancer_ucl),
              if (cred) sprintf("The gap is credibly %s in cancer-related threads (shift %s, pd %.3f).",
                                dir, or3(r$shift_or, r$shift_lcl, r$shift_ucl), r$shift_pd)
              else sprintf("No credible difference (shift %s, pd %.3f).",
                           or3(r$shift_or, r$shift_lcl, r$shift_ucl), r$shift_pd)))
}
```

Here too the same caveats apply: a borderline interval (one end close to 1)
is weak evidence, and the cancer flag itself comes from a language model.
